Two meta-analysis examples: a mean case and a standard deviation (SD) case

Source: vignettes/two-meta-analyses.Rmd
two-meta-analyses.Rmd
library(fivenumMeta)
has_mm <- requireNamespace("metamedian", quietly = TRUE)  # the SD case's data
has_mf <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)     # confirms the pooling

What the two cases show

This vignette assumes that the reader knows what se_imputed_diff() and se_imputed_df() return: each study’s imputed mean and SD with their naive and exact standard errors, in the columns that vignette("fivenumMeta") describes. Start there if the columns, the scenarios or the conventions are new.

Wu, Shi and Tong (2026) illustrate the exact standard errors on two published meta-analyses, and this vignette runs both with the package. In a meta-analysis of means in which three of six studies report the median and the range, the exact standard errors raise the pooled standard error by 7.1%. In a meta-analysis of SDs in which 29 of 51 studies report the quartiles, they raise the pooled standard error by 35% and bring I2I^2 from 86% to 70%. Both data sets are public. The vitamin D studies ship with this package as the data set vitd, and the age studies come with the metamedian package as its data set dat.age. Every number in this vignette is computed when it is built.

Both cases pool with the common-effect model. Study ii gives an effect estimate yiy_i with variance viv_i, and the model weights it by wi=1/viw_i = 1/v_i: θ̂=∑iwiyi∑iwi,SE(θ̂)=(∑iwi)−1/2,𝒬=∑iwi(yi−θ̂)2,I2=max⁡{0,𝒬−(K−1)𝒬}, \hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad \mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) = \Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^{-1/2}, \qquad \mathcal Q = \sum_i w_i (y_i - \hat\theta)^2, \qquad I^2 = \max\Big\{0, \frac{\mathcal Q - (K - 1)}{\mathcal Q}\Big\}, where KK is the number of studies. 𝒬\mathcal Q and I2I^2 are the heterogeneity measures of Higgins and Thompson (2002).

We run each meta-analysis twice: with the naive standard errors, which treat the imputed mean and SD as a sample mean and SD, and with the exact standard errors computed from the exact standard deviation factors, which this package takes from the moments of the normal order statistics of the osmoments package (Wu and Tong, 2026). That is, the two analyses share the yiy_i and differ only in the viv_i. The function pool_imputed() computes the four quantities above twice from the output of se_imputed_diff(), once with the naive and once with the exact standard errors, and prints the two fits side by side. Both cases call it.

A meta-analysis of means from medians and ranges

The data are the meta-analysis of serum vitamin D (nmol/L) in tuberculosis cases against controls of Nnoaham and Clarke (2008), typed from their Table 1 and shipped with this package as the data set vitd. Three studies report the median, minimum and maximum of each group, two a sample mean and SD, and one a mean with the minimum and maximum.

vitd
#>               study n.cases min.cases med.cases max.cases mean.cases sd.cases
#> 1        Davies, UK      40      2.25     16.00     74.25         NA       NA
#> 2 Grange, Indonesia      40     43.75     65.75    130.50         NA       NA
#> 3     Davies, Kenya      15     16.75     39.75     89.25         NA       NA
#> 4  Davies, Thailand      51        NA        NA        NA      69.50     24.5
#> 5   Chan, Hong Kong      22        NA        NA        NA      46.50     18.5
#> 6 Sasidharan, India      35      2.50        NA     75.00      26.75       NA
#>   n.controls min.controls med.controls max.controls mean.controls sd.controls
#> 1         40         9.00        27.25       132.50            NA          NA
#> 2         38        48.50        69.50       125.00            NA          NA
#> 3         15        26.25        65.50       114.75            NA          NA
#> 4         51           NA           NA           NA         95.50       29.25
#> 5         23           NA           NA           NA         52.25       15.75
#> 6         16        22.50           NA       145.00         48.50          NA

The study that reports a mean with the range (Sasidharan, India) has no SD. se_imputed_df() reads such a row as the scenario mean_range: the mean is kept as the sample mean, and the SD is imputed from the two extremes alone, as the range divided by the expected range of a normal sample of that size, which is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of the SD from the extremes. Its exact standard error is the standard deviation of that estimator, from the moments of the two extremes. The standard error of this study’s mean is then σ̂/n\hat\sigma/\sqrt n under both calculations, with the imputed SD plugged in.

The call takes the controls first, so the difference yi is controls minus cases, as the paper reports it. Each group’s factors are taken at its own sample size, exact at the even sizes 40 and 38, where the reported median is the average of the two middle values under R’s default quantile definition. The table lists each study’s scenario, its difference with the two standard errors, and its weight in percent under each.

d <- se_imputed_diff(vitd, suffixes = c(".controls", ".cases"))
fit_vd <- pool_imputed(d)
tab <- data.frame(study = d$study, scenario = d$scenario.cases,
                  yi = d$yi, se_naive = d$sei_naive, se_exact = d$sei,
                  w_naive = fit_vd$weights$naive,
                  w_exact = fit_vd$weights$exact)
print(tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
#>              study   scenario    yi se_naive se_exact w_naive w_exact
#>         Davies, UK         S1 15.42     5.23     6.01   19.30   16.77
#>  Grange, Indonesia         S1  3.04     4.30     4.93   28.57   24.89
#>      Davies, Kenya         S1 22.91     8.51     9.34    7.29    6.94
#>   Davies, Thailand     sample 26.00     5.34     5.34   18.49   21.20
#>    Chan, Hong Kong     sample  5.75     5.13     5.13   20.04   22.97
#>  Sasidharan, India mean_range 21.75     9.15     9.15    6.31    7.23
fit_vd
#> Pooled difference of means (group 1 minus group 2), common-effect model (EE), 6 studies
#>          estimate    se ci.lb ci.ub      pval     Q    I2
#> naive SE    12.85 2.298 8.346 17.35 2.240e-08 15.77 68.29
#> exact SE    13.34 2.460 8.517 18.16 5.876e-08 14.18 64.75
#> 95% confidence intervals and p-values from the normal distribution. Q has 5 degrees of freedom, and I2 is in percent.
#> The weights in percent are $weights. Every field with str() or unclass().

Compared with the naive calculation, the exact calculation raises the standard errors of the three studies that report the median and the range by 9.8% to 14.8%, the inflation of the imputed mean under that scenario at these sample sizes. Their share of the weight falls from 55% to 49%. The pooled difference moves from 12.8 to 13.3 nmol/L, and its standard error from 2.30 to 2.46, a rise of 7.1%, so its confidence interval widens by the same proportion.

A meta-analysis of SDs from quartiles

A meta-analysis of variability studies whether an outcome is more dispersed in one group than in another. Here the effect size is the log variability ratio of Nakagawa et al. (2015), the log of the ratio of the two groups’ SDs, yi=log⁡(σ̂i1/σ̂i2)y_i = \log(\hat\sigma_{i1}/\hat\sigma_{i2}). The data are the 51 studies of the age of COVID-19 nonsurvivors (group 1) against survivors (group 2) of Katzenschlager et al. (2021), shipped with the metamedian package as its data set dat.age: 29 report the three quartiles and 22 a sample mean and SD in both groups. The question is whether age is less dispersed among those who died. measure = "lnVR" gives yiy_i with its two standard errors in place of the difference of means.

d <- se_imputed_diff(metamedian::dat.age, measure = "lnVR")  # suffixes .g1, .g2
table(d$scenario.g1)
#> 
#>     S2 sample 
#>     29     22
fit_vr <- pool_imputed(d)
fit_vr
#> Pooled log variability ratio (SD of group 1 over SD of group 2), common-effect model (EE), 51 studies
#>          estimate      se   ci.lb   ci.ub      pval     Q    I2
#> naive SE  -0.2253 0.01610 -0.2568 -0.1937 1.768e-44 346.6 85.58
#> exact SE  -0.2152 0.02167 -0.2577 -0.1728 2.939e-23 165.3 69.75
#> 95% confidence intervals and p-values from the normal distribution. Q has 50 degrees of freedom, and I2 is in percent.
#> exp() of the estimate and of the limits gives the ratio of SDs.
#> The weights in percent are $weights. Every field with str() or unclass().

The variance of yiy_i is approximated by the sum of one term per group, to first order in each group’s SD (the delta method, Var(log⁡X)≈Var(X)/(EX)2\mathrm{Var}(\log X) \approx \mathrm{Var}(X)/(\mathrm{E}X)^2). The naive calculation gives every group the large-sample term of a sample SD of nn normal observations, 1/{2(n−1)}1/\{2(n - 1)\}. The exact calculation keeps that term for a group that gives its sample SD and uses Cσ2(n)C^2_\sigma(n), the exact variance of the imputed SD in units of σ2\sigma^2, for a group whose SD is imputed from the quartiles, which the output carries as (se_sigma / sigma_hat)^2: vinaive=12(ni1−1)+12(ni2−1),viexact=t(ni1)+t(ni2),t(n)={1/{2(n−1)}for a sample SD,Cσ2(n)for an imputed SD. v_i^{\mathrm{naive}} = \frac{1}{2(n_{i1} - 1)} + \frac{1}{2(n_{i2} - 1)}, \qquad v_i^{\mathrm{exact}} = t(n_{i1}) + t(n_{i2}), \qquad t(n) = \begin{cases} 1/\{2(n - 1)\} & \text{for a sample SD,} \\ C^2_\sigma(n) & \text{for an imputed SD.} \end{cases} The columns sei_naive and sei are the square roots of these two variances. Both are first-order approximations of the variance of a log, so the intervals below are normal approximations. The bias correction of the log ratio of Nakagawa et al. (2015) is not applied, as in Wu, Shi and Tong (2026). Both analyses use the plain log ratio.

For a group whose SD is imputed from the quartiles, Cσ2(n)C^2_\sigma(n) is 2.34 to 2.72 times the naive term 1/{2(n−1)}1/\{2(n - 1)\}. Under the exact variance, the share of the weight on the 29 quartile studies falls from 72% to 49%. The pooled log ratio changes little, from -0.225 to -0.215, so the SD of age among nonsurvivors is about 0.80 times that among survivors either way. Its standard error, however, rises by 35%, from 0.0161 to 0.0217, and its confidence interval widens by the same proportion. 𝒬\mathcal Q falls from 346.6 to 165.3, and I2I^2 from 86% to 70%. Since the two fits share the yiy_i and differ only in the variances, the fall in 𝒬\mathcal Q and I2I^2 comes from the larger within-study variances alone: the extra spread of an imputed SD, which the naive variance leaves out, was counted as heterogeneity.

With the metafor package, the exact fit is rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d, method = "EE"), which returns the same pooled estimate, standard error and 𝒬\mathcal Q, and the naive fit takes sei_naive in the same way:

f <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d, method = "EE")
c(estimate = as.numeric(f$b), se = f$se, Q = f$QE, I2 = f$I2)
#>     estimate           se            Q           I2 
#>  -0.21524814   0.02166619 165.27554705  69.74749085

Can we predict the severe course of COVID-19, a systematic review and meta-analysis of indicators of clinical outcome? PLOS One 16, e0255154.
